answer_text:
# Finding $\lim_{t \to \infty} e^{At}$

## Setting Up with the Jordan Form

Since $A$ is a square matrix, it has a Jordan canonical form: $A = PJP^{-1}$, so

$$e^{At} = P\,e^{Jt}\,P^{-1}$$

The matrix $J$ is block-diagonal with Jordan blocks $J_i = \lambda_i I + N_i$ (where $N_i$ is nilpotent/strictly upper-triangular). Thus:

$$e^{J_i t} = e^{\lambda_i t}\,e^{N_i t} = e^{\lambda_i t}\!\left(I + N_i t + \frac{N_i^2 t^2}{2!} + \cdots\right)$$

## Analyzing Each Jordan Block as $t\to\infty$

| Condition on $\lambda_i$ | Behavior of $e^{J_i t}$ |
|---|---|
| $\operatorname{Re}(\lambda_i) < 0$ | $e^{\lambda_i t}\to 0$ polynomially $\implies$ **block $\to 0$** |
| $\operatorname{Re}(\lambda_i) > 0$ | $e^{\lambda_i t}\to\infty$ $\implies$ **diverges** |
| $\operatorname{Re}(\lambda_i) = 0,\;\lambda_i\neq 0$ | $e^{\lambda_i t}$ oscillates $\implies$ **no limit** |
| $\lambda_i = 0,\;N_i\neq 0$ | polynomial growth in $t$ $\implies$ **diverges** |

## Conclusion

The limit $\lim_{t\to\infty} e^{At}$ **exists and equals the zero matrix** if and only if **every eigenvalue of $A$ has strictly negative real part**:

$$\operatorname{Re}(\lambda_i) < 0 \quad \text{for all } i.$$

Under this (standard stability) condition, every Jordan block $e^{J_i t}\to 0$, so $e^{Jt}\to 0$, and therefore $e^{At} = Pe^{Jt}P^{-1}\to 0$.

If any eigenvalue has non-negative real part, the limit fails to exist (the entries either grow without bound or oscillate).

$$\boxed{0}$$
